meaning: Something has continued from a point in the past up to now. Written and a little emotional.

senses.label: Ever since ...
senses.meaning: Describes how things have been from the time something happened until now. The second half is usually an ongoing state, or experience such as 「一度も〜ない」 (never once). The tone is formal and reflective. It sounds more old-fashioned than 「〜て以来」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + このかた (common: 「生まれてこのかた」, 「来てこのかた」)
examples: I have never once been abroad in my whole life.
Ever since I came to Japan, I have lived in this town.
I haven't seen him since I quit the company.

notes: The second half must be a state that has lasted from then until now, or whether something has ever happened, such as 「一度も〜ない」. It cannot be a one-time action: ✕「日本に来てこのかた、富士山に登った」→ ○「日本に来てから、富士山に登った」.
The starting point must be something that has already happened in the past. It can't refer to the future or to something that just happened: ✕「卒業してこのかた、留学したい」 ✕「昨日来てこのかた」.
It must follow the te-form: ✕「生まれたこのかた」→ ○「生まれてこのかた」.
The tone is old-fashioned and reflective, so it sounds affected in casual chat. In conversation people usually say 「〜てから（ずっと）」 or 「〜て以来」.
Written with the kanji 「この方」, it looks the same as 「この方」 meaning “this person”. 「生まれてこの方」 means “since I was born”, not “this person who was born”. Check whether the preceding word is in the te-form.

daily.title: Talking about food habits
daily.description: Telling a friend about your life so far.
daily.example: I've never eaten natto in my whole life.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Common in a character's monologue looking back on the past.
daily.example: Since I left my hometown, I haven't seen my mother's face.

work.title: Anniversary speech
work.description: A company president looks back at an anniversary ceremony.
work.example: Ever since our founding, we have held to the principle of quality first.

etymology: 「この方（かた）」 originally meant “this side, this direction”. It came to mean “the time from then until now”. So 「〜てこのかた」 means “from doing ... until now”. It is an old-fashioned written expression.

similar.title: 〜て以来
similar.explanation: The meaning is almost the same: “ever since ..., continuously ...”. 「〜て以来」 is the neutral, common written form and can also attach directly to nouns (「入社以来」). 「〜てこのかた」 is more old-fashioned and usually carries a reflective feeling, most often in 「生まれてこのかた」.

similar.title: 〜てからというもの
similar.explanation: 「〜てからというもの」 stresses that the event was a turning point and things changed a lot afterwards (「子どもが生まれてからというもの、生活が一変した」). 「〜てこのかた」 focuses on something continuing up to now, often with 「一度も〜ない」, and does not necessarily involve a change.

formation: 「〜てこのかた」 = te-form + 「この」 + 「方（かた）」. 「方」 originally means a direction or side, so 「この方」 is “this side”. Used for time, it means “the period up to this side (the present)”. The te-form marks the completed action as the starting point, so the whole thing reads “after doing A, up to this side, now”, i.e. “ever since A”. Because the endpoint is fixed at the present, the second half naturally describes a state continuing to today, or whether something has ever happened, as with 「一度も〜ない」. Using 「方」 for time is an old-fashioned usage, which gives the whole expression its formal, reflective tone.

meaning: Because a state or feeling is so extreme, a result follows.
connection: あまりの + noun (a 「〜さ」 noun or an emotion noun) + に／で

senses.label: So ... that
senses.meaning: Because the degree is too great, the result in the second half happens. The result is usually an involuntary reaction: being speechless, crying, fainting. 「に」 is more common; 「で」 is a bit more casual.
senses.connection: あまりの + noun (「暑さ」, 「寒さ」, 「痛み」, 「驚き」, 「ショック」, etc.) + に／で
examples: It was so hot that I lost my appetite.
The pain was so bad I couldn't even make a sound.
The shock was so great that I was at a loss for words.

senses.label: Something shocking
senses.meaning: 「あまりのことに」 means the event was too outrageous or unexpected. It often shows a person being stunned or not knowing what to do.
senses.connection: あまりのことに + reaction (「言葉が出ない」, 「呆然とする」, etc.)
examples: It was such a shock that for a while I couldn't think at all.

notes: After 「あまりの」 there must be a noun, so adjectives have to be nominalized first: ✕「あまり暑いに」 ✕「あまりの暑いに」→ ○「あまりの暑さに」.
The second half is an involuntary reaction (being speechless, crying, fainting). It can't be a volitional act, request or command: ✕「あまりの暑さに、エアコンをつけてください」→ ○「あまりに暑いので、エアコンをつけてください」.

Don't confuse it with 「あまり〜ない」 (not very ...), which pairs with a negative: 「あまりの寒さに震えた」 means “I shivered from the extreme cold”, while 「あまり寒くない」 means “it isn't very cold”. The meanings are opposite.
The 「余り」 in 「余りの布」 or 「余りの時間」 means “leftover”, and is not this grammar point.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with a friend in summer.
daily.example: It was so hot yesterday that I didn't step outside once.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A report on a crowded festival.
daily.example: There were so many people that the station was packed.

daily.title: A happy surprise
daily.description: Describing how you felt getting an unexpected gift.
daily.example: I was so happy that I cried.

work.title: Incident report
work.description: Explaining a problem caused by construction work.
work.example: The noise was so loud that nearby residents complained.

etymology: 「あまり」 comes from the verb 「余る」 (to be left over, to exceed). It means “beyond the limit”. 「あまりの + noun」 is “a ... beyond the limit”, and 「に／で」 marks the cause.

similar.title: 〜あまり
similar.explanation: They share a source, both coming from 「余る」. 「〜あまり」 follows a verb or 「noun + の」 (「心配するあまり」, 「心配のあまり」) and mostly describes a bad result caused by excessive emotion or behavior. 「あまりの〜に」 puts 「あまりの」 before a noun and stresses that the degree of some state or feeling was too much to bear (「あまりの暑さに」).

formation: 「あまり」 is the noun form of the verb 「余る」 (to exceed, to be left over) and means “the part beyond the limit”. So 「あまりの + noun」 means “... beyond the limit” (「あまりの暑さ」 = heat that went beyond the limit). The following 「に」 marks the cause that triggers a reaction, the same 「に」 as in 「知らせに驚く」; 「で」 marks a general cause. Together it means “because the degree went past the limit, ...”. Since “going past the limit” is something imposed on the person from outside, the second half is usually a reaction the person can't control rather than a deliberate action. And because the two parts are joined by 「の」, only a noun can come before it, so adjectives must become 「〜さ」.

meaning: First accept a statement or fact, then point out that reality doesn't match it: “That said, ...”.
connection: Noun / plain form + とはいうものの; at the start of a sentence: 「とはいうものの、」

senses.label: Although it's said that ...
senses.meaning: Accepts the first part, but the reality differs from what you'd expect. The second half is often something disappointing or the actual situation. Written, but also used in speech.
senses.connection: Noun / verb or adjective plain form + とはいうものの (「だ」 is usually dropped after nouns and na-adjectives)
examples: It may be spring, but the cold days continue.
Although I practice every day, I'm just not getting better.
It may be cheap, but it's too expensive for students.

senses.label: That said, ...
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, links to what came before: “Having said that, ...”. You can also say 「そうはいうものの」.
senses.connection: Sentence start: とはいうものの、／そうはいうものの、
examples: I started a diet. That said, I can't give up sweets.
It's better to decide soon. Having said that, it's not easy to decide.

notes: There must be a gap between expectation and reality. The second half is a reality that doesn't match what the first half leads you to expect: ✕「春とはいうものの、暖かい日が続く」→ ○「春とはいうものの、まだ寒い日が続く」.
The second half generally can't contain the speaker's volition, a command or a request: ✕「春とはいうものの、コートを着ていきなさい」→ ○「春とはいえ、コートを着ていきなさい」.
The 「いう」 here is only a form. It doesn't mean someone actually said something, so don't translate it as “somebody says”.
At the start of a sentence you must say 「とはいうものの、」 or 「そうはいうものの、」. You can't say just 「ものの」: ✕「ダイエットを始めた。ものの、…」.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.example: It may be autumn according to the calendar, but it's still really hot, isn't it?

daily.title: Making fun of yourself
daily.description: Telling a friend about a plan you gave up.
daily.example: I decided to run every morning. That said, it ended after three days.

work.title: Sales report
work.description: Explaining the current situation at a meeting.
work.example: Although sales are recovering, they still haven't reached the target.

work.title: News commentary
work.example: Although the economy is said to have recovered, few people actually feel it.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + topic particle 「は」 + 「いう」 + the contrastive 「ものの」. Literally “although one says ...”. 「ものの」 comes from the formal noun 「もの」 + 「の」 and was already used for contrast in classical Japanese.

similar.title: 〜ものの
similar.explanation: They share a source: 「とはいうものの」 is 「ものの」 with 「とはいう」 added. 「〜ものの」 follows the plain form directly and is the general “although ..., but ...”. 「〜とはいうものの」 adds a sense of “it's called ... / nominally ...”, and is often used when the name doesn't match reality.

similar.title: 〜とはいえ
similar.explanation: The meaning is almost the same, and it can also begin a sentence. 「とはいえ」 is more concise and more formal, and the second half can also contain advice or volition (「春とはいえ、コートを持って行きなさい」). 「とはいうものの」 is mostly followed by a reality that falls short of expectations.

similar.title: 〜といっても
similar.explanation: 「〜といっても」 focuses on “the actual degree isn't that high”, and is used to correct an overly high impression the listener might have (「料理ができるといっても、卵焼きくらいです」). It is common in speech. 「〜とはいうものの」 focuses on reality not matching expectation and is more bookish.

formation: 「〜とはいうものの」 = the quotative 「と」 + the contrastive 「は」 + 「いう」 + the concessive 「ものの」. 「Aという」 first puts A forward as a label or nominal claim (“it is said to be A”), and 「は」 sets that claim against the actual situation. 「ものの」 means “although ... (but)”. Together: “although nominally called A, in reality ...”. Because it first grants a label, the first half is often a season, a status, a name or a recognized fact, and the second half is a reality that doesn't match the expectation created by it. If you drop 「とはいう」 and say just 「ものの」, only the plain concessive remains, without the flavor of “people say so”.

meaning: Once a certain topic comes up (usually something a person cares a lot about), their attitude or behavior changes from usual.
connection: Noun + の + こととなると／ことになると

senses.label: When it comes to ...
senses.meaning: Whenever the topic involves something, a person acts differently than usual. The subject is usually a person. The second half is often “gets serious, gets passionate, loses their cool”.
senses.connection: Noun + のこととなると／のことになると (also 「〜のこととなれば」, 「〜のことになったら」)
examples: When it comes to baseball, my father suddenly starts talking forever.
When it comes to her kids, she can't stay calm.
My usually quiet brother becomes a different person when it comes to cars.

senses.label: When it comes to doing ...
senses.meaning: After a verb's dictionary form, it means “when it's time to do ...”, the second half happens. Less common.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + こととなると
examples: When it comes to speaking in front of people, I always get nervous.

notes: To mark a topic it must be 「noun + の + こととなると」. It can't attach directly to a noun: ✕「野球こととなると」→ ○「野球のこととなると」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ことになる」 for decisions: 「転勤することになると、家族と離れる」 means “if it's decided that I'll be transferred”, not “when it comes to transfers”. Only 「noun + のこと」 means “when it comes to ...”.
The second half describes a person's habitual reaction or character (becoming a different person, talking a lot). It can't be a one-time fact or the speaker's volition: ✕「野球のこととなると、明日見に行こう」.

This pattern often carries a teasing note of “loses all sense of proportion when it comes to ...”. Telling your boss 「部長はゴルフのこととなると人が変わりますね」 to his face may sound rude. You could say 「ゴルフにはお詳しいですね」 instead.

daily.title: Introducing your family
daily.description: Telling a friend about your father's hobby.
daily.example: When it comes to fishing, my dad's eyes light up.

daily.title: Talking about a friend
daily.description: Discussing a mutual friend's personality with a classmate.
daily.example: When it comes to money, he suddenly gets stingy.

work.title: Introducing a senior colleague
work.description: Telling a new hire about a strict coworker.
work.example: When it comes to quality, Tanaka-san never compromises.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「こと」 + 「となる／になる」 (to become) + the conditional 「と」. Literally “once it becomes a matter of ...”, which came to mean “once the topic turns to ...”.

similar.title: 〜となると
similar.explanation: They share a source: 「こととなると」 is 「となると」 with 「（の）こと」 added. 「〜となると」 can express the supposition “if it comes to ...”, followed by a judgment or decision (「留学するとなると、お金がかかる」). 「〜のこととなると」 refers specifically to a person's attitude changing as soon as a topic touches on something.

similar.title: 〜にかけては
similar.explanation: Both talk about how a person performs in some area. 「〜にかけては」 praises ability, and the second half is often 「誰にも負けない」 or 「右に出る者はいない」. 「〜のこととなると」 focuses on a change of attitude (becoming eager, losing composure) and doesn't necessarily mean the person is good at it.

similar.title: 〜ことになる
similar.explanation: They share a source, both built from 「こと + になる」. 「〜ことになる」 follows a verb and expresses a decision or outcome (「来月転勤することになった」). 「〜のことになると」 follows 「noun + の」, where 「こと」 means “matters concerning ...”, and marks a topic. The connection differs, so the meaning is completely different.

formation: 「〜こととなると」 = the formal noun 「こと」 + 「となる／になる」 (to become) + the conditional particle 「と」. 「Aのこと」 means “matters related to A”, and 「となると」 means “once it becomes a case of ...”. Together: “once the topic or matter becomes one about A”, i.e. “when it comes to A”. The conditional 「と」 expresses “whenever ..., inevitably ...”, so the second half is a reaction that appears every time, which suits describing a person's habits or character. If a dictionary-form verb comes before it, 「こと」 means “the act of doing ...”, giving “when it comes to the point of doing ...”.

meaning: Shows a way of doing something, a method, or an appearance: “like this / in such a way”.
connection: こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな / verb plain form / sentence + という + ふうに

senses.label: In ... way
senses.meaning: Shows a concrete way or method. Common as 「こんなふうに」, 「そんなふうに」, 「どんなふうに」. Very common in speech and more casual than 「〜ように」.
senses.connection: こんな／そんな／あんな／どんな + ふうに; この／その／あの／どの + ふうに
examples: You can write it like this.
I don't know how I should explain it.
You don't have to say it like that.

senses.label: Like this (summing up)
senses.meaning: 「〜というふうに」 sums up the concrete items listed before it: “in this way”. Often used to explain division of work, order, or rules.
senses.connection: Sentence / noun + というふうに
examples: We take turns, with A on Monday, B on Tuesday, and so on.
Please proceed like this: first greet everyone, then get to the main topic.

senses.label: Look / attitude
senses.meaning: 「〜ふうな」 or 「〜ふうに」 after a verb means “looking as if ..., with the attitude of ...”. It often suggests pretending.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form / nai-form / te-iru form + ふうな／ふうに (「知ったふうな口をきく」)
examples: He laughed as if he knew nothing.
Don't talk like you know it all.

notes: For demonstratives use 「こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな」 or 「こういう」: ✕「こうふうに」 ✕「これふうに」→ ○「こんなふうに」「こういうふうに」.
「知ったふうな口をきく」 and 「分かったふうなことを言う」 are strongly derogatory, meaning “pretend to know” or “act like a know-it-all”. They would be very rude to say about a superior or a client.
「ふうに」 is rather colloquial. In reports, papers and official documents it can look casual, and writing usually switches to 「〜ように」 or 「〜という形で」.
「noun + 風」 (「和風」, 「サラリーマン風の男」) means “-style, -looking”. It is not the same as 「〜というふうに」, which summarizes a way of doing something.

daily.title: After an argument
daily.description: Feeling hurt by a friend's words.
daily.example: It makes me sad when you say things like that.

work.title: Assigning tasks
work.description: A boss explains how work is divided.
work.example: Let's split it up like this: phones in the morning, documents in the afternoon.

work.title: Checking how to do something
work.description: Asking a senior colleague how to fill in a form.
work.example: How should I fill out this document?

etymology: 「風（ふう）」 originally meant “wind”. It came to mean “custom, style, appearance”. 「〜ふうに」 means “in the manner of ...”.

similar.title: 〜風（ふう）
similar.explanation: They share a source, both coming from 「風」. 「noun + 風」 means “in the style of ... / looking like ...” (「和風」, 「学生風の男」). 「〜ふうに」 follows a demonstrative or a clause and expresses a way or manner.

similar.title: 〜ような・〜ように・〜みたいな（comparison / example）
similar.explanation: 「〜ように」 can also express manner (「先生が言ったように書く」) and is more bookish and neutral. 「ふうに」 is more colloquial, often pairs with 「こんな・そんな」, and puts more weight on the concrete way something is done and how it looks.

similar.title: 〜ふりをする
similar.explanation: After a verb, 「〜ふうに」 can mean “in the manner of pretending ...” (「知らないふうに笑う」), close to 「〜ふりをする」. 「ふりをする」 clearly means deliberate pretending, while 「ふうに」 only says “it looks that way”, so the sense of pretending is weaker.

formation: 「ふう」 is the on-reading of the kanji 「風」. Its original meaning is “wind”, which extends through “custom, fashion” to “style, appearance, manner”. 「〜ふうに」 = 「ふう」 (appearance, manner) + the manner-marking 「に」, i.e. “in the manner of ...”. Before it, 「こんな・そんな」 points to a concrete manner; with 「という」, a whole stretch of content is packaged as “this kind of approach”, so 「〜というふうに」 suits summarizing lists, divisions of work and sequences. 「ふうな」 is the form that modifies a noun. Because an “appearance” may be only on the surface, after a verb (「知らないふうに」) it takes on the sense of “looking like” or “pretending”.

meaning: The second half holds true regardless of the first part. It isn't affected by that condition.

senses.label: Regardless of ...
senses.meaning: The second half holds no matter what the first part is. The noun before it usually covers several possibilities, like 「天候」, 「年齢」, 「経験の有無」. Formal; common in rules and notices.
senses.connection: Noun + にかかわりなく; “verb dictionary form + its negative” + にかかわりなく (「行く行かないにかかわりなく」)
examples: Anyone can apply, regardless of age or experience.
The game will be held as scheduled regardless of the weather.
Whether or not you will attend, please be sure to reply.

senses.label: Unrelated to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜とはかかわりなく」 means “with no connection to ...”. 「〜にかかわりのない」 modifies a noun: “unrelated to ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + とはかかわりなく; noun + にかかわりのない + noun
examples: This matter was decided without regard to his wishes.
Please save conversations unrelated to work for later.

notes: No 「も」 comes before it: 「天候にかかわりなく実施する」 means “we'll hold it regardless of the weather”. Saying 「雨にもかかわらず実施した」 instead means “it was held even though it rained”, with a sense of surprise, so the meaning is completely different.
The first half must be a word that can be divided into several cases, or opposing items in pairs. It can't be a single fixed fact: ✕「70歳にかかわりなく」→ ○「年齢にかかわりなく」.
When pairing affirmative and negative, both sides must be stated: ✕「参加するにかかわりなく」→ ○「参加するしないにかかわりなく」「参加するかどうかにかかわりなく」.
The tone is written and formal, used mostly in notices and rules. It sounds stiff when chatting with friends, where people usually say 「〜に関係なく」.

daily.title: Community event notice
daily.description: A flyer explains who can join.
daily.example: Anyone can take part, regardless of experience.

daily.title: Reading a shop sign
daily.description: Opening hours posted at a store entrance.
daily.example: We open at ten every day, regardless of the day of the week.

work.title: Job posting
work.description: A company explains its hiring criteria.
work.example: We hire based on ability, regardless of nationality or gender.

work.title: Contract terms
work.example: The monthly fee is fixed, regardless of how often you use the service.

etymology: 「かかわり」 is the noun form of the verb 「かかわる（関わる・係わる）」 (to be related). Adding 「なく」 (without) gives “without any relation”.

similar.title: 〜にかかわらず
similar.explanation: They share a source, both coming from 「関わる」, and the meaning is nearly the same and mostly interchangeable. 「にかかわらず」 is the most common. 「にかかわりなく」 is built from the noun 「かかわり」, so it feels more like “no connection at all”, and you can also say 「とはかかわりなく」.

similar.title: 〜を問わず
similar.explanation: It means “regardless of ... / without distinguishing ...” and is mostly used in hiring and recruitment, often after paired or classifiable words such as 「男女」, 「年齢」 and 「国籍」. 「にかかわりなく」 has a wider range and often follows a 「する・しない」 pair.

similar.title: 〜によらず
similar.explanation: 「〜によらず」 means “not depending on ...”. It also has fixed phrases such as 「見かけによらず」 (contrary to appearances) and can mean “not relying on a certain means”. 「にかかわりなく」 only means “regardless of ...”.

formation: 「〜にかかわりなく」 = 「に」 (the object concerned) + 「かかわり」 (the nominalized continuative form of the verb 「関わる」, meaning “connection, involvement”) + 「なく」 (the continuative form of 「ない」, used as an adverb). Literally it is “without connection to ...”. All the cases listed in the first half have “no connection” to the second half, so it means “regardless of ..., ...”. It has the same source as 「にかかわらず」: the latter negates the verb with the classical negative 「ず」, while this one uses the noun 「かかわり」 + 「ない」, saying “no relation” more directly. Precisely because 「かかわり」 is a noun, you can say 「〜とはかかわりなく」 and 「〜にかかわりのない + noun」.

meaning: 「お／ご + verb + 申し上げる」 is a humble expression even more formal than 「お〜する」.
connection: お + verb masu-stem / ご + kango (Sino-Japanese) verbal noun + 申し上げる

senses.label: Very formal humble
senses.meaning: Lowers your own action to show respect to the other person. More formal than 「お〜する」 or 「お〜いたす」. Common in letters, speeches, business emails, and announcements.
senses.connection: お + native verb masu-stem (お願い・お祈り・お詫び) / ご + kango noun (ご案内・ご報告・ご説明) + 申し上げます
examples: I wish everyone good health.
I sincerely apologize for the trouble we caused you.
Allow me to explain our upcoming schedule.

senses.label: Set phrases for greetings and condolences
senses.meaning: Fixed expressions for congratulations, sympathy, thanks, and condolences, such as 「お喜び申し上げます」, 「お見舞い申し上げます」, 「お悔やみ申し上げます」.
senses.connection: お喜び／お祝い／お見舞い／お悔やみ／御礼 + 申し上げます
examples: Respectful wishes for a happy New Year.
Wishing you well in the summer heat.
Please accept my deepest condolences.

notes: It can only be used for your own side's actions. Used for the other person's action, it belittles them: ✕「お客様がご説明申し上げます」→ ○「お客様がご説明くださいます」. (When speaking to a client about a superior at your own company, it can be used: 「部長の田中がご説明申し上げます」.)
The action must be directed toward the other person. It can't be used for your own actions that don't involve them: ✕「お昼をお食べ申し上げます」.
Use 「ご」 with Sino-Japanese words and 「お」 with native Japanese words: ✕「お説明申し上げます」→ ○「ご説明申し上げます」 (exceptions such as 「お電話」 and 「お礼」).
Don't stack other humble forms into excessive honorifics: ✕「お祈り申し上げさせていただきます」→ ○「お祈り申し上げます」.

Be careful with set phrases: 「お悔やみ申し上げます」 is only for a death in the other person's family. When the other person is in mourning (「喪中」), don't send a 「謹んで新春のお喜び申し上げます」 New Year's card; people generally send a 「寒中お見舞い申し上げます」 card instead.

daily.title: Writing a New Year's card
daily.description: A New Year's card to a teacher or an older person.
daily.example: Thank you very much for all your kindness over the past year.

daily.title: At a funeral
daily.example: Please accept my heartfelt condolences on your loss.

work.title: Business email
work.example: We deeply apologize for the inconvenience.

work.title: Ceremony speech
work.example: We sincerely thank you all for coming today.

etymology: 「申し上げる」 combines 「申す」 (humble form of 「言う」) and 「上げる」. It originally meant “to speak up to a superior”. Later it joined with 「お／ご + verb」 to form a formal humble pattern.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する（humble）
similar.explanation: The construction is the same, both being 「お／ご + verb + humble verb」. 「お〜する」 is the general humble form and is common in everyday business conversation. 「お〜申し上げる」 is more formal and mostly used in letters, speeches and formal apologies, and fewer verbs go with it (「お持ち申し上げる」 sounds unnatural).

similar.title: 参る・申す・いたす（special humble verbs）
similar.explanation: They share a source: 「申し上げる」 comes from 「申す」 among them. Used alone, 「申す」 and 「申し上げる」 are the humble forms of 「言う」 (「先ほど申し上げたとおり」). When they follow 「お／ご〜」 to form this pattern, they no longer mean “say” but add a formal, humble tone to the whole action.

formation: 「お〜申し上げる」 = the prefix 「お／ご」 + the continuative form of a verb (or a Sino-Japanese verbal noun) + 「申し上げる」. 「申し上げる」 is made from 「申す」 (the humble form of 「言う」) + 「上げる」 (to raise or offer upward), and originally means “to state to, or present to, someone of higher rank”. An action involving the other person (a wish, an apology, an explanation) is first turned into a noun form with 「お／ご」, then 「申し上げる」 expresses “respectfully presenting it to the other person”, which adds a layer of looking up to them that 「お〜する」 lacks. Because the core meaning is “presenting to the other person”, the action must be directed at them. That is also why it pairs most often with verbs that convey feelings, such as wishing, apologizing, thanking, congratulating and offering condolences, forming many fixed phrases in letters and speeches.

meaning: Uses a feature or fact as the basis or reason for a name, a judgment, or a result.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, noun + である + ところから

senses.label: Origin of a name
senses.meaning: Explains why something got its name or why a saying arose. The second half is often 「〜と呼ばれる」 or 「〜と名付けられた」. Written style.
senses.connection: Plain form + ところから (common: 「〜ているところから」, 「〜であるところから」)
examples: Because its shape resembles Mt. Fuji, this mountain is called Tsugaru Fuji.
Because there used to be many oil shops here, this slope was named Abura-zaka (Oil Slope).

senses.label: Basis for a judgment
senses.meaning: Makes an inference from a fact or a sign. The second half is often 「〜と考えられる」, 「〜と分かった」, or 「〜と判断した」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ところから + expression of guessing or judgment
examples: Since the window was open, it's thought that the culprit got in here.
From the way his voice was shaking, I could tell he was nervous.

notes: Don't confuse it with the place-marking 「ところから」: 「高いところから飛び降りる」 means “jump down from a high place”. In this grammar point, the first half is a clause describing a feature or sign, and the second half is a naming or judgment.

Don't confuse it with 「〜たところ」 (“when I did ..., I found ...”): 「調べたところ、ミスが分かった」 means “when I checked, I found a mistake”, expressing a discovery in sequence. 「〜ところから」 expresses a basis, and the second half is mostly 「〜と呼ばれる」 or 「〜と考えられる」.
The second half is a naming or inference. It can't contain the speaker's volition or a request: ✕「天気がいいところから、出かけましょう」→ ○「天気がいいから、出かけましょう」.
After a noun, use 「noun + である + ところから」: ✕「港町ところから」→ ○「港町であるところから」.

daily.title: Listening to a tour guide
daily.description: A guide explains where a place name comes from.
daily.example: This area has many cherry trees, so it's called Sakura-machi.

daily.title: Reading a mystery novel
daily.description: A detective reasons from the clues.
daily.example: Since his shoes were wet, we can guess he walked here in the rain.

work.title: Investigation report
work.description: Explaining the basis for a judgment about a problem.
work.example: Since we have received several similar complaints, we judged it highly likely that the product is defective.

work.title: Academic article
work.description: Explaining where the name of a technique comes from.
work.example: This technique is called the Italian method because it originated in Italy.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally meant “place”, and came to mean “a point, an aspect”. With 「から」 marking a starting point, it means “starting from this point”: the basis for a name or judgment.

similar.title: 〜ことから
similar.explanation: The meaning is almost the same and they are mostly interchangeable, both expressing the origin of a name or the basis of a judgment. 「〜ことから」 is the most common. 「〜ところから」 is more bookish and slightly stresses “one particular point or feature”, and appears often in explanations of how place names and object names came about.

similar.title: 〜ところを見ると
similar.explanation: They share a source, both using 「ところ」 to mean “situation, feature”, and both express the basis of a judgment. 「〜ところを見ると」 infers from something you saw with your own eyes, and the second half takes 「らしい」 or 「ようだ」. 「〜ところから」 is also often used for the origin of names besides inference, and is more bookish.

similar.title: 〜からすると
similar.explanation: It also expresses the basis of a judgment, but it mostly follows a noun (「表情からすると」, 「彼の性格からすると」) and can also mean “from the standpoint of ...”. 「〜ところから」 follows a clause, takes one concrete fact as its basis, and doesn't express a standpoint.

formation: 「〜ところから」 = the formal noun 「ところ」 + the starting-point 「から」. 「ところ」 originally means “place”; as a formal noun it refers to “a point, aspect or feature” of something. 「から」 means “starting from ...”. Together: “starting from this point”, i.e. taking the first half as the starting point for naming or inferring. Because the starting point is “a feature”, the first half mostly describes appearance, nature or signs (「形が似ている」, 「声が震えている」), and the second half is the name or judgment that follows (「〜と呼ばれる」, 「〜と考えられる」). This is also how it differs from 「から」 expressing a plain cause: the emphasis is on the “basis”, not the “direct cause”.
